business_description: HP Inc. is a global technology company operating in more than 170 countries. It sells devices, services and subscriptions spanning personal computing, printing, 3D printing, hybrid work, gaming and related technologies. Personal Systems includes commercial and consumer desktops, notebooks, workstations including AI PCs and workstations, thin clients, retail POS systems, displays, hybrid systems, software, endpoint-security solutions and lifecycle services. Commercial customers include enterprises, public-sector organizations and SMBs; Consumer PS targets individual consumers. Printing provides consumer and commercial printer hardware, supplies, services and solutions, including office, home, graphics, industrial and 3D printing. ([SEC][1]) FY2025 revenue was $55,295 million: Personal Systems $38,532 million, Printing $16,702 million and Corporate Investments $62 million. Commercial PS contributed $27,438 million, Consumer PS $11,094 million, Supplies $10,916 million, Commercial Printing $4,633 million and Consumer Printing $1,153 million. ([SEC][1]) FY2025 geographic revenue was Americas $23,545 million, Europe/Middle East/Africa $18,596 million and Asia-Pacific/Japan $13,154 million. ([SEC][1]) Products represented $52,002 million of FY2025 revenue versus $3,293 million from services. ([SEC][1]) Pricing-power evidence is mixed. FY2025 Personal Systems revenue rose 6.5% as units rose 4.3% and ASPs rose 3.1%, with HP attributing higher ASPs partly to disciplined pricing; however, Personal Systems operating margin fell because higher commodity and tariff costs outweighed pricing actions. ([SEC][1]) In Q3 FY2026 Personal Systems revenue rose 18% but units fell 16% and operating margin was 4.6%, while Printing revenue fell 2%, units fell 7%, and Printing retained an 18.1% operating margin. ([HP Investor Relations][2])
moat_evidence: Intangible Assets: HP reported more than 16,000 patents worldwide as of October 31, 2025 and states that it seeks patent protection where proprietary rights can maintain or improve its competitive position. ([SEC][1])

Intangible Assets / Brand and ecosystem: HP identifies its broad portfolio, innovation and R&D capabilities including security features, design, brand, procurement leverage, ability to cross-sell, service/support capabilities, product accessibility and broad distribution strategy as competitive advantages. ([SEC][1])

Low-Cost Production / operating scale: HP uses outsourced manufacturers worldwide specifically to generate cost efficiencies, reduce time to market and preserve supply-chain flexibility. Its build-to-order process is described as maximizing manufacturing and logistics efficiencies through high-volume basic configurations. The filings do not provide peer cost comparisons proving HP is structurally the industry's lowest-cost producer. ([SEC][1])

Switching Costs: HP offers lifecycle services, configurations, deployment, extended warranties, managed solutions and Device-as-a-Service, and some services agreements contain early-termination penalties. However, HP also states those penalties may not fully cover its investment and that customers can terminate implementations or decline additional services, so the filings support some contractual friction but not evidence of uniformly high switching costs. ([SEC][1])

growth_driver_evidence.sales_marketing: HP reported FY2025 SG&A expense of $5,821 million, but the filings do not separately disclose sales-and-marketing investment or quantify incremental marketing spend specifically intended to acquire new customers. ([SEC][1])
growth_driver_evidence.distribution_channels: HP sells through resellers, distribution partners, systems integrators, retailers and direct online sales. The majority of total revenue is generated through channel resellers, while HP manages direct online sales and channel relationships for consumers and other customer groups. The filings describe broad existing routes to market rather than a separately quantified newly launched distribution channel. ([SEC][1])
growth_driver_evidence.geographic_expansion: A specific new-country expansion is not disclosed. Adjacent-market expansion is disclosed: HP is investing in endpoint services and Device-as-a-Service, accelerating hybrid-system adjacencies, expanding subscription printing through Instant Ink and HP All-In Plan, providing digital-printing solutions for industrial graphics applications, and expanding its 3D-printing footprint across digital manufacturing and strategic applications. ([SEC][1])
growth_driver_evidence.acquisitions: No material acquisition is identified in the provided FY2026 filings as a major growth driver. For the first nine months of FY2026, HP reported $10 million of cash paid in connection with a business acquisition and $26 million of proceeds from a business divestiture, but the filings do not provide evidence sufficient to assess whether that acquisition was value-accretive. ([HP Investor Relations][2])
growth_driver_evidence.pricing_power: Evidence is mixed rather than demonstrating unrestricted pricing power. FY2025 Personal Systems ASPs increased 3.1%, with disciplined pricing cited as a contributor, while units increased 4.3%; however, segment margin fell as tariff and commodity costs outweighed pricing actions. ([SEC][1]) By Q3 FY2026, Personal Systems revenue was up 18% but units were down 16% and segment operating margin was 4.6%, demonstrating that higher revenue and price/mix did not translate into volume retention or margin expansion. Printing retained an 18.1% Q3 FY2026 operating margin despite a 2% revenue decline and 7% unit decline. ([HP Investor Relations][2])
growth_driver_evidence.new_products: HP disclosed a new line of AI PCs and workstations designed for local AI processing, intelligent-print features across home, office and graphics solutions, its Omni consumer PC portfolio, and strategic emphasis on Device-as-a-Service, Instant Ink, HP All-In Plan, Managed Print Services, industrial digital printing and 3D printing. ([SEC][1])
growth_driver_evidence.customer_retention: The filings do not disclose a customer-retention or churn percentage. Supplies are consumables designed for recurring use in installed Printing hardware, providing evidence of repeat purchasing from the installed base. HP also has service arrangements, although it explicitly states that customers may terminate implementations, discontinue services or decline additional services. ([SEC][1])

risk_evidence.concentration: TD SYNNEX Corp. accounted for 12% of HP's FY2025 net revenue; no single customer represented 10% or more in FY2024 or FY2023. TD SYNNEX also represented 12.6% of gross accounts receivable at October 31, 2025 versus 9.7% a year earlier. The ten largest distributor/reseller receivable balances collectively increased from 38% to 47% of gross accounts receivable. ([SEC][1])
risk_evidence.disruption: HP states that technology changes can make products uneconomical or obsolete and that it must continually develop and enhance products because product life cycles are short. ([SEC][1]) AI is simultaneously an opportunity and a disruption vector: HP already sells AI PCs and workstations and incorporates intelligent-print functions, while its filings warn that rapidly evolving technology and competitors can affect demand. ([SEC][1]) Printing faces structural substitution and installed-base risks: HP's strategy increasingly emphasizes subscriptions, digital industrial printing and 3D printing, while recurring Supplies economics remain dependent on continuing use of installed hardware. ([SEC][1])
risk_evidence.outside_forces: HP is materially exposed to commodity/component costs, tariffs, foreign exchange, interest rates and supply availability. The FY2025 filing specifically identifies increasing memory and storage costs, tariff costs and uncertainty over customers' ability to absorb price increases. ([SEC][1]) HP also relies on single-source suppliers for important components, including Canon for certain laser printer engines and toner cartridges and Intel, AMD and NVIDIA for processors. ([SEC][1]) HP mitigates foreign-exchange and interest-rate exposure with forward contracts, options, treasury-rate locks, swaps and other derivatives; FY2025 foreign-currency cash-flow hedge notional value was about $14.5 billion. ([SEC][1]) In FY2026, the U.S. Supreme Court decision invalidating certain IEEPA tariffs enabled HP to seek approximately $0.3 billion of tariff refunds, of which $127 million had been received by July 31 and another $91 million subsequently. ([SEC][3])
risk_evidence.competition: HP describes both principal businesses as highly competitive and subject to price competition. Personal Systems competitors named in the filing include Acer, Apple, ASUS, Dell, Huawei, Lenovo, Logitech, Microsoft, Samsung and Toshiba. Printing competitors include Brother, Canon, Pantum, Epson, Ricoh and Xerox; HP also competes with lower-priced imitation, refill and remanufactured supplies. ([SEC][1]) HP says it expects to continue adjusting prices to remain competitive and notes that some competitors may have better component pricing, terms, allocation or economies of scale. ([SEC][1]) The filings do not disclose comparable peer operating margins, so no filing-supported relative-margin advantage can be asserted.

price_sentiment_narrative: The latest filings do not provide a complete trailing-12-month share-price narrative through September 2026 or disclose sell-side analyst sentiment. HP's FY2025 filing does provide historical shareholder-return information through October 31, 2025, while subsequent filings focus on operating results rather than stock-market sentiment. Filing-supported bull evidence includes Q3 FY2026 revenue of $15.7 billion, up 12.5% year over year, Q3 free cash flow of $1.6 billion, Personal Systems revenue growth of 18%, raised FY2026 EPS guidance and raised FY2026 free-cash-flow guidance to $3.0-$3.2 billion. ([HP Investor Relations][2]) The bull case is also supported by AI-PC/workstation product expansion, premium-product initiatives, subscriptions and HP's productivity program. Filing-supported bear evidence includes Q3 Personal Systems units falling 16% despite 18% revenue growth, only a 4.6% Personal Systems operating margin, Printing revenue falling 2%, Printing units falling 7%, and dependence on price/mix amid elevated memory and component costs. ([HP Investor Relations][2]) FY2025 had already shown net earnings declining to $2,529 million from $2,775 million even as revenue rose from $53,559 million to $55,295 million. ([SEC][1])

ai_risk_evidence.liability: HP's core products include physical PCs, workstations, printers, supplies, POS systems, displays and hybrid systems, with lifecycle support and warranty obligations. The filings identify potential product defects, reliability, warranty, cybersecurity and technology-performance risks, but do not quantify the cost of an individual AI-generated error or establish that continuous human oversight is indispensable. Because most current revenue relates to physical devices and supplies rather than autonomous decision-making software, the filings do not support treating AI-error liability as the principal threat to the existing revenue base. ([SEC][1])
ai_risk_evidence.business_model: HP's current reported business is predominantly product-based rather than seat-based. FY2025 Products revenue was $52,002 million versus $3,293 million of Services revenue; HP defines Products as hardware, supplies, subscriptions and software licenses and Services as service offerings and hardware support. ([SEC][1]) Therefore the filings support describing the business as primarily linked to devices, units, supplies and usage rather than per-employee software seats. The exact seat-based subscription portion is not separately disclosed.
ai_risk_evidence.physical_world: HP has substantial physical-world exposure. It sells PCs, workstations, displays, POS systems, printers and consumable supplies and uses outsourced manufacturers globally to produce HP-designed products, while also manufacturing some finished products from acquired components and subassemblies. ([SEC][1]) AI cannot eliminate the physical manufacturing, component sourcing, logistics and device-fulfillment requirements associated with this reported revenue mix.
ai_risk_evidence.network: The filings document substantial proprietary intellectual property, including more than 16,000 patents, but they do not disclose a proprietary-data network effect comparable with a marketplace or platform whose value rises directly with user participation. ([SEC][1]) Not disclosed in the provided filings whether HP possesses a proprietary data asset that an external AI system would need in order to replicate its core economics.

capital_return_evidence.current_shares_outstanding: 901,790,969 common shares outstanding as of August 19, 2026. ([SEC][3])
capital_return_evidence.shares_repurchased_last_3_fy: FY2025: approximately 29.6 million shares; FY2024: approximately 62.9 million shares; FY2023: approximately 3.6 million shares. The statement of stockholders' deficit reports reductions of 29.623 million, 62.856 million and 3.624 million shares respectively. ([SEC][1])
capital_return_evidence.buyback_spend_last_3_fy: FY2025: approximately $850 million cash used for repurchases; FY2024: approximately $2.1 billion; FY2023: approximately $100 million. ([SEC][1])
capital_return_evidence.remaining_buyback_authorization: Approximately $7.7 billion remained under HP's Board-approved share-repurchase authorization as of July 31, 2026, down from approximately $8.4 billion at October 31, 2025. ([SEC][3])
capital_return_evidence.dividend_per_share_last_3_fy: FY2025: $1.16 per common share; FY2024: $1.10; FY2023: $1.05. ([SEC][1]) HP increased its quarterly dividend to $0.30 beginning in FY2026, and paid $0.30 per share in Q3 FY2026. ([HP Investor Relations][4])
capital_return_evidence.free_cash_flow_last_3_fy: FY2025: $2.9 billion; FY2024: $3.3 billion; FY2023: $3.1 billion. HP defines free cash flow as operating cash flow adjusted for net investments in integrated-financing leases and net investments in property, plant, equipment and purchased intangibles. ([HP Investor Relations][4])
capital_return_evidence.capital_return_policy: HP continues to use cash generated by operations to fund operations, capital expenditure, debt obligations, dividends and authorized share repurchases. ([SEC][3]) Capital return has varied with available free cash flow: HP returned approximately 37% of FY2023 FCF through repurchases and dividends, approximately 96% in FY2024 and approximately 66% in FY2025. ([SEC][5]) Buybacks have materially exceeded equity issuance on a net-share basis recently: shares outstanding on the balance sheet declined from 988.8 million at FY2023 to 939.0 million at FY2024, 921.1 million at FY2025 and 903.4 million at July 31, 2026. ([SEC][1]) Stock-based compensation was $522 million in FY2025, and the 2026 proxy disclosed potential dilution from equity incentive plans increasing from 6.3% to 14.3% if the amended plan was approved, so gross buybacks should not be treated as equivalent to the net reduction in shares. ([SEC][1])

governance_evidence.promoter_pledging_pct: Not disclosed in the provided filings
governance_evidence.related_party_transactions: HP's related-person policy requires review of transactions exceeding $120,000 in which a related person has a material interest and directs the governance committee to consider whether terms are comparable with those available to unaffiliated third parties. ([SEC][6]) For FY2025 HP disclosed an approximately $2.15 million transaction with Greenwave Holdings Inc., in which director Richard L. Clemmer held a 30% equity interest, covering adoption of Greenwave technology over a five-year period. HP explicitly described the transaction as arm's-length. ([SEC][6])
governance_evidence.promoter_shareholding_trend: HP is a U.S. public company and the filings do not use an Indian-style promoter-shareholding classification. As of December 31, 2025, all current directors, director nominees and executive officers as a group beneficially owned 1,679,955 shares, less than 1% of shares outstanding. The provided filings do not give a comparable 3-5 year insider-group ownership series from which a reliable trend can be calculated. ([SEC][6])
governance_evidence.insider_transactions: The July 2026 10-Q disclosed that Anneliese Olson, President of Imaging, Printing & Solutions, adopted a Rule 10b5-1-type written plan on June 4, 2026 for the future sale of up to 170,929 shares underlying time-based RSUs and associated dividend-equivalent units, scheduled to commence October 29, 2026 and expire no later than March 31, 2027. ([SEC][3]) HP's proxy also states that employees and directors are prohibited from hedging HP securities and, with limited exceptions, executives are prohibited from pledging HP securities or holding them in margin accounts. ([SEC][6])
governance_evidence.capital_allocation_track_record: The current filings do not provide enough evidence to classify HP's acquisition history overall as value-accretive or value-destructive. They do disclose that FY2025 acquisition/divestiture charges declined to $45 million as integration activity decreased, and FY2025 included $65 million of impairment charges related to acquired Printing customer contracts, customer lists and distribution agreements plus $27 million related to acquired technology and patents in Corporate Investments. ([SEC][1]) HP also continued servicing debt associated with its 2022 Poly acquisition. ([SEC][1]) These disclosures show that some acquired intangible assets required impairment, but the provided filings do not establish an overall acquisition return sufficient for a broader value-creation judgment.
governance_evidence.accounting_disclosure_red_flags: Ernst & Young LLP has served as HP's auditor since 2000. EY issued an unqualified opinion on HP's FY2025 consolidated financial statements and concluded internal control over financial reporting was effective at October 31, 2025. ([SEC][1]) HP had disclosed a material weakness in FY2024 involving reliance on information from software systems without effectively designed IT general controls around access, change management and job-schedule monitoring; management concluded that this weakness had been remediated by October 31, 2025. ([SEC][1]) No restatement or delayed FY2025 filing is disclosed in the provided filings.

bear.assumption: Analyst judgment. Assume 5-year revenue CAGR of -1.0% and FY+5 net margin of 3.3%. The bear path assumes Q3 FY2026's price/mix-led Personal Systems revenue growth proves unsustainable: higher ASPs continue masking falling unit volumes, PC replacement demand weakens after the Windows refresh, memory/component costs remain elevated, and Printing's installed-base, Supplies and hardware-unit declines accelerate. Printing margin falls meaningfully below its recent high-teens level and productivity savings fail to fully compensate. The filing anchors are Q3 FY2026 Personal Systems units down 16%, Printing units down 7%, Printing revenue down 2%, and Personal Systems operating margin only 4.6%. ([HP Investor Relations][2]) Assume net shares decline only 1.0% annually because weaker FCF limits repurchases, and an average annual dividend of $1.20 per share remains fundable. A 7x exit P/E reflects a mature, shrinking earnings profile; the provided filings do not disclose HP's historical P/E range, so the multiple is analyst judgment rather than a filing-derived historical-range observation.

base.assumption: Analyst judgment. Assume 5-year revenue CAGR of 2.5% and FY+5 net margin of 4.5%. The base case assumes Personal Systems normalizes after the Windows-refresh and current price/mix cycle, AI PCs and premium commercial devices provide moderate mix support rather than explosive growth, Printing revenue continues to decline slowly but operating margin stays broadly in the mid-to-high teens, and endpoint services/subscriptions grow gradually from a small base. HP's FY2026-FY2028 productivity program offsets part of commodity and structural pressure. Current anchors include Q3 FY2026 revenue growth of 12.5%, raised FY2026 FCF guidance of $3.0-$3.2 billion, and Printing operating margin of 18.1%. ([HP Investor Relations][2]) Assume net share count declines 2.0% annually, below the aggressive FY2024 repurchase pace and consistent with maintaining buybacks within roughly $3 billion annual FCF after dividends, and average annual dividends of $1.30 per share. A 10x exit P/E assumes HP remains a mature hardware and supplies company with stable rather than structurally improved economics; the provided filings do not disclose a historical P/E range.

bull.assumption: Analyst judgment. Assume 5-year revenue CAGR of 4.5% and FY+5 net margin of 5.8%. Numeric hurdles are: Personal Systems operating margin must recover from Q3 FY2026's 4.6% toward at least roughly 6%; Printing operating margin must remain at approximately 17%-19% despite secular revenue pressure; annual FCF should sustainably exceed roughly $3.5 billion; AI PCs, workstations, premium commercial devices, endpoint services, subscriptions and hybrid systems must generate growth sufficient to more than offset declining traditional Printing; and net shares must continue falling without buybacks consuming more cash than FCF can support. HP's current strategic focus on AI PCs/workstations, Device-as-a-Service, Instant Ink, Managed Print Services and 3D/digital printing provides the filing-supported growth mechanisms. ([SEC][1]) Assume net share count declines 2.5% annually and average annual dividends of $1.40 per share. A 13x exit P/E requires a genuine quality improvement—more recurring/services revenue, restored Personal Systems margins and durable Printing profitability—not merely higher cyclical PC earnings. The filings do not disclose HP's historical P/E high, so 13x is analyst judgment rather than a claim that it is within a disclosed historical range.
